entry.evidence: further improvement of both the theoretical and practical functions of the model is needed

steps.action: Frame the problem from the literature: degree-day models lack physical mechanisms and need improvement for simulating snowmelt under forest canopies of differing openness. The aim of improving the model for subcanopy snowmelt is restated on p. 3.
steps.quote: further improvement of both the theoretical and practical functions of the model is needed

steps.action: Take from other groups the expectation that, under the canopy, the gain in longwave radiation can exceed the loss of shortwave radiation and so dominate snowmelt.
steps.quote: the increase in longwave radiation can even exceed the decrease in shortwave radiation

steps.action: Design the field setup: an open sunny-slope station (100%) and four shady-slope stations at 20%, 30%, 40% and 80% canopy openness; openness is measured from fisheye photographs with Gap Light Analyzer.
steps.quote: as well as shady slopes in areas with differing degrees of openness

steps.action: Measure snowmelt with a galvanized-iron lysimeter weighed every 2 h (2010) and a tipping-bucket gauge (2012, 2013), and record meteorology with TRM-ZS2 automatic weather stations; filter the data to 20:00-20:00 days and merge nearby stations to remove instrument outliers.
steps.quote: The snowmelt rate was obtained using two methods: a snow lysimeter (observed snowmelt rate) and calculations derived

steps.action: Adopt two established rivals: the traditional temperature-only degree-day model (Model 1, Finsterwalder and Schunk) and the degree-day model with net shortwave radiation (Model 2, Pellicciotti et al. 2005).
steps.quote: The degree-day model is generally in the form of that first formulated by Finsterwalder and Schunk (1887)

steps.action: Construct Model 3: the degree-day model plus a net longwave radiation term and a water recession term driven by the previous day's snowmelt.
steps.quote: An improved degree-day model was constructed based on air temperature, net longwave radiation and water recession.

steps.action: Compute subcanopy net longwave radiation through a forward model: Stefan-Boltzmann grey bodies weighted by openness (Essery et al. 2008), the Iziomon emissivity, cloud cover from humidity, and snow-surface temperature from air temperature, with air temperature standing in for canopy temperature.
steps.quote: (in this study, the air temperature was used instead of canopy temperature)

steps.action: Fix the evaluation design: R2, Ens and PBIAS with rating thresholds taken from Tan et al. (2021); calibrate on 2013 data and verify on 2010 (100% site) and 2012 (20% and 80% sites) data.
steps.quote: the 2013 data were used for model correction and parameter calibration

steps.action: Report the microclimate and snowmelt patterns across openness. Forest sites have lower shortwave and higher net longwave radiation, and calm winds. Snowmelt is slower at higher openness early in the season and faster late in the season.
steps.quote: The net longwave radiation in the forest-covered areas was significantly higher than that of the open side

steps.action: Calibrate Model 1 (degree-day factor) at all five stations on 2013 data.
steps.quote: Model 1 was simulated using the relevant data from five stations

steps.action: Compare Model 1 with observations: it performs best at 80% openness, degrades as openness falls, and is rated not satisfied at the open site and at 20% openness.
steps.quote: the simulated results for the open site was “not satisfied”

steps.action: Calibrate Model 2 (degree-day factor and shortwave coefficient) at the three stations with shortwave data (20%, 80%, 100%).
steps.quote: Model 2 was simulated using the data from three stations

steps.action: Compare Model 2 with observations: it is good to very good at the open site and at 80% openness, but not satisfied at 20% openness.
steps.quote: The 20% forest canopy openness area using Model 2 therefore produced result as “not satisfied”.

steps.action: Reject the shortwave-augmented model as adequate for low-openness subcanopy sites.
steps.quote: the degree-day model that includes shortwave radiation still needs to be improved for subcanopy areas with a lesser degree of forest canopy [...]

steps.action: Calibrate Model 3 (degree-day factor, longwave coefficient b, recession constants c and d) at all five stations on 2013 data.
steps.quote: [...] was simulated using the relevant data from five stations

steps.action: Compare Model 3 with Models 1 and 2. R2 rises by 5-45% and Ens by 2-41% over Model 1, and R2 by 5-35% over Model 2. At 20% openness R2 rises from 0.45 to 0.90.
steps.quote: Compared with Model 1, the results simulated by Model 3 showed that R2

steps.action: Verify Model 3 with the 2013 parameters on held-out years (2010 at 100%, 2012 at 20% and 80%), giving R2 0.88-0.96. A suspect data point (17 April 2013) is dropped to show the effect on the metrics.
steps.quote: Model verification was carried out using data from three stations

steps.action: Attribute the residual early-season overestimates and peak-melt underestimates to auxiliaries rather than to Model 3. Named causes are snowpack water-holding capacity, omitted topographic longwave radiation, and lysimeter iron-box heating by penetrating radiation.
steps.quote: the heating of the iron box used to measure snowmelt by penetrative radiation

steps.action: Fit the degree-day factor of Model 3 against canopy openness across the four forest stations (R2 = 0.67) and compare with Kuusisto's 0.51; note that the open site does not fit the relation.
steps.quote: the correlation between the degree-day factor and the degree of forest canopy openness increased to 0.67

steps.action: Compare the Model 3 degree-day factors with published Tianshan values (Zhang et al. 2006b; Gan et al. 2022; Ma and Cheng 2003) and explain the lower values by the added radiation and recession terms.
steps.quote: reported that the snow degree-day factor of Tianshan Mountain was 3.1

steps.action: Estimate an observed water recession coefficient from night-time (20:00-08:00) snowmelt as a fraction of daily melt (Eq. 13) at each openness.
steps.quote: The actual water recession value was taken to be the quantity of snowmelt observed at night.

steps.action: Compare the simulated recession term of Model 3 with the observed recession. The trends agree but the simulated recession is too large, which the authors attribute to an incomplete energy term and to the night-only measurement assumption.
steps.quote: the simulated value was consistent with the trend in the actual observed value, but also that the simulated water recession was larger

steps.action: Add topography-emitted longwave radiation as an extra component and quantify its share at each openness (1.4-27.5% of canopy longwave); the snowmelt simulation is not significantly improved.
steps.quote: the simulation effect of the snowmelt process was not significantly improved after adding additional topographic radiation as a parameter

steps.action: Check the premise that air temperature can replace canopy temperature, by regressing air temperature on stem temperature at the 30% and 40% sites (R2 0.94 and 0.97).
steps.quote: this study used air temperature instead of canopy temperature, due to the complexity of the calculation

steps.action: Keep Model 3 as a more reliable, simple method for simulating subcanopy snowmelt across canopy openness, and propose more stations and remote sensing for basin-wide use.
steps.quote: the improvement of the degree-day model using air temperature, net longwave radiation and the water recession process was clear

tree.answer: Subcanopy snowmelt differs from open-site melt; longwave radiation and night-time water recession are thought to matter under canopy
Snowmelt and radiation are observed directly at stations; degree-day factors and recession coefficients are inferred by calibration
Improve a conceptual degree-day snowmelt model for forest subcanopy
Three nested rival models: temperature only (Model 1), plus shortwave (Model 2), plus longwave and recession (Model 3)
The rivals differ in fit quality, especially at low canopy openness
Conditions found: natural canopy openness at five stations, not set

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats the melt season (2010, 2012, 2013); held-out years are used for verification
Model 3 holds on held-out years at three stations (R2 0.88-0.96); adding topographic longwave brings no significant gain
Model 3 kept; Models 1 and 2 judged inadequate at low openness

end.claim: Adding net longwave radiation and a water recession term to the degree-day model gives a simple subcanopy snowmelt model whose performance is characterized: calibration R2 0.83-0.96 at five stations, and verification R2 > 0.88, Ens > 0.87, PBIAS 0.63-8.44% at three stations.

decisive_move.sentence: The claim rests on comparing the calibrated Model 3 with Models 1 and 2 at stations of differing openness: the large gain at 20% openness (R2 0.45 to 0.90) is what singles out the longwave and recession terms.

gates.evidence: Action: stations were placed across canopy openness, which reflects the published expectation that canopy effects on radiation matter (pp. 2, 4). But the observations span 2010-2013, and nothing states that the Model 3 hypothesis directed their acquisition (inference). Claim: Model 3 was scored on held-out years and could have failed (p. 10). However, the verification covers only three stations (11-13 days each at 20% and 80%), and only Model 3 was verified, not the rivals. Model 3 also has more free parameters than Models 1 and 2, with no penalty applied. Registration: the rating thresholds were taken from Tan et al. (2021) (p. 6). The calibration/validation split was chosen from data continuity (p. 7), and no pre-specification is stated.

imports.item: Stefan-Boltzmann law for grey-body longwave emission from sky, canopy and snow
Hemispherical (fisheye) canopy photography analysed with Gap Light Analyzer to measure canopy openness

limits:
No review file was supplied, so the review history is unknown. The XML text held only the abstract and captions, so body steps are cited by printed page.

Sub-claims at other statuses:
(a) The degree-day factor increases with canopy openness: regularity_in_range, R2 = 0.67 across four forest stations only, with the open site excluded as non-conforming (p. 11).
(b) Longwave radiation dominates over shortwave in the low-openness subcanopy: best_explanation, from radiation observations and model fit, not a decisive test (§0 ¶3; p. 10).
(c) Topographic longwave radiation can be ignored at low openness: best_explanation (p. 13).

Internal inconsistencies:
- Conclusion 1 says mean daily temperature was higher in forested areas (p. 14), but the Results report it lower (p. 7).
- Conclusion 3 says topographic longwave radiation improved simulations at high openness (p. 14), but Section 5.3 reports no significant improvement (p. 13).
- The 100% verification discussion refers to 17 April 2013 data, although that site was verified on 2010 data (pp. 7, 10).

Design limits:
- Models 1 and 2 were not verified on held-out years.
- Model 2 could not be run at 30% and 40% openness for lack of shortwave data.
- The snowmelt instrument changed between 2010 (lysimeter) and 2012/2013 (tipping bucket) with no stated cross-calibration.
- The simulated recession term was larger than the observed recession, and this mismatch is unresolved (p. 13).
- The authors give no data availability (p. 15).
- Whether the parameter count of Model 3 inflates its fit gain is not examined (inference).
